props.title: I Wish
props.initialSlug: Two brothers plot to reunite their split family

sections.content: **I Wish** (2011) represents Japanese director Hirokazu Kore-eda at his most optimistic, crafting a tender exploration of childhood dreams through the story of two separated brothers hoping to reunite. Like his masterpiece Nobody Knows (2004), Kore-eda demonstrates an uncanny ability to direct child actors with naturalistic performances that never feel forced. The film shares DNA with great child-perspective classics like **The 400 Blows** (1959) and **My Neighbor Totoro** (1988), capturing that delicate balance between youthful wonder and real-world limitations.

sections.content: The high-speed bullet train serves as both literal plot device and metaphor in **I Wish**, connecting the film to Japan's rich tradition of train movies like **The Yellow Handkerchief** (1977) and **Departures** (2008). Kore-eda uses the railway to explore themes of progress versus tradition, while the children's belief in the magical properties of passing trains echoes the magical realism found in early Miyazaki works like **Castle in the Sky** (1986).

Working with real-life brothers Koki and Ohshirô Maeda gives **I Wish** an authenticity that elevates it beyond typical coming-of-age fare. Their natural chemistry recalls other great sibling performances like those in **Yi Yi** (2000) and **Ponette** (1996). The film's Kagoshima setting provides a backdrop of active volcanoes and regional traditions that Kore-eda uses to contrast childhood imagination with environmental reality. sections.content: **I Wish** continues a long tradition of Japanese films examining childhood with remarkable sensitivity, from Ozu's **I Was Born, But...** (1932) to Kore-eda's own **After Life** (1998). Where many Western coming-of-age films focus on rebellion or loss of innocence, Japanese cinema often explores the quiet moments of discovery and the bittersweet nature of growing up, as seen in contemporary works like **Summer Wars** (2009) and **Wolf Children** (2012).
